summary: History of Indian broker failures (Karvy, BMA) and the trust problem of brokers holding client funds; explains SEBI's ASBA-style reform planned for secondary market margins, the old 2.5% then Rs.100/lot brokerage era, and the 'peak margin penalty' deduction myth.
lessons: Brokers holding client funds create deduction disputes; ASBA-style blocking keeps money in your bank until needed.
A per-order fee matches the broker's actual effort; per-share brokerage on options was wildly disproportionate.
If money never leaves your bank account, refund fights disappear - that is the point of the ASBA model.
Regulators should enable business growth; some rules (extra margin on long-dated options) backfire and shrink liquidity.

summary: Full explainer: bond yield mechanics (price vs yield), normal upward-sloping curve, and why short-yield-over-long-yield inversion has preceded recessions (1998, 2006, 2019, 2022). Links Fed rate hikes, helicopter money, SVB collapse, and advises shifting toward fixed instruments during inversion regimes.
lessons: Yield curve inversion (short-term yield above long-term) has preceded every modern US recession - a macro red flag, not a timing tool.
When short-term rates are unusually high, fixed instruments beat equity; tilt allocation defensively.
Raising rates fights demand-pull inflation, but post-COVID inflation came from printed helicopter money - the medicine and disease mismatch.
When the US tightens, emerging economies must follow or watch their currency slide - India cannot decouple.

summary: Explains the Fed's post-COVID dilemma: helicopter money caused inflation; rate hikes 'continue until something breaks' - SVB collapsed like Lehman, Yellen first refused then arranged backstops, Credit Suisse hit record lows. Fed talks markets up and down (hawkish/dovish zigzag); Nifty doing 2000-point round trips until the pivot.
lessons: When the Fed starts hiking, 'it will not stop until something breaks' - plan for the accident, not the landing.
Central banks now manage markets both ways: hawkish talk to cap rallies, dovish rescue at lows - trade the zigzag, not the narrative.
Helicopter money created a supply-shock-proof inflation that rates alone cannot quickly fix.
In credit crises the announced position (no bailout) reverses within hours - never position on official first statements.

title_clean: The Rise and Fall of IT Stocks in India
summary: Why IT - historically a defensive, currency-hedge sector - collapsed in 2023: its BFSI clients (SVB, First Republic, Credit Suisse-UBS) were the epicentre of the banking crisis; mergers deleted customers; high rates forced software budget cuts and contract repricing despite rupee 72→83. Advises SIP for 3-5 year investors, no lumpsum.
lessons: Defensive-sector logic (IT gains from rupee depreciation) breaks when the sector's clients are the ones failing.
Mergers among clients shrink the customer base - consolidation in client industries is a silent revenue risk.
In client-budget crunches, currency windfalls get clawed back via contract repricing - short-term FX gains are not durable.
Long-term SIP into beaten sectors beats lumpsum when the macro overhang (US rates) has not peaked.

strategies.name: Sector entry discipline (SIP vs lumpsum)
strategies.construction: Long-term (3-5yr) investors: SIP into top IT names (Infosys, TCS, Wipro); momentum investors wait for dust to settle; lumpsum avoided
strategies.numbers: 1-yr to 23-Mar-2023: Nifty -1.38%, IT index -22.38%, Wipro -40%, Mphasis -43%, Infosys -27%, LTTS -31%; rupee 72→83; FII sales ~40-45k crore/month Dec 2021-Jun 2022

strategies.risks: structural decline vs cyclical trough is unknowable in advance; SIP mitigates timing risk
